writing.exampleCaption: The closure counter shows the difference: two calls for the total, and the search stops after one more.
writing.explanation:
`orders.filter(...).map(...).reduce(...)` runs each stage over the whole array and allocates an intermediate array between stages. Rust's `orders.iter().filter(...).map(...).sum()` first builds a description of the work. Nothing happens until `sum` asks for the first item; then each order flows through `filter` and `map` one at a time, with no intermediate `Vec`.

Laziness changes what runs. In the JavaScript example, `map(...).find(...)` calls the mapping function for all three orders before `find` looks at one. The Rust pipeline stops at the first match, so its closure runs once. A pipeline that is never consumed does nothing at all, which is why rustc warns that an unused `Map` must be used in the practice code.

The names mostly carry over: `map`, `filter` and `find` are the same, `some` is `any`, `every` is `all`, `reduce` with an initial value is `fold`, and `flatMap` is `flat_map`. The length of a filtered result is `count()`, and `collect::<Vec<_>>()` gives you a collection back. There is no index argument; add `.enumerate()` to get `(index, item)` pairs.

Watch what the iterator yields. `iter()` yields references (`&Order`), `iter_mut()` yields `&mut Order`, and `into_iter()` on a `Vec` yields owned values and consumes the vector. That is why the closures read `o.cents` through a reference, and why `find(|&c| c > 1000)` destructures the `&u64` it receives.
writing.feedback: An adapter only describes work. Without a consumer the closure never runs, and rustc warns that the `Map` must be used.
writing.question: In the practice code, what has `map` done by the time `done` prints?

recall.answer: `map 1`, `map 2`, then `Some(20)`. `find` pulls one item at a time and stops at the first match, so the closure never runs for `3`. An array's `map` would have logged all three before searching.
recall.question: What does this print, and why not three `map` lines?

recall.answer: `any`, `all`, `fold(initial, |acc, x| ...)` and `flat_map`. As in JavaScript, `any` and `all` short-circuit. Unlike the array methods, they work on any iterator, and the adapters before them run lazily.
recall.question: What are the Rust names for `some`, `every`, `reduce` with an initial value, and `flatMap`?

writing.rule: Iterator adapters are lazy: a consumer such as `sum`, `find`, `collect` or a `for` loop drives the work, one item at a time.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness passes every case, including the number of `price_of` calls and an empty slice. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: `map` and `filter` on an array run at once and build new arrays; Rust's iterator adapters do nothing until a consumer such as `sum`, `find` or `collect` pulls values.
